questions.stem: A 21 year old man was struck on the right temple by a golf ball. He was knocked out for about 30 seconds, then got up, chatted to friends and drove home. Three hours later his partner finds him drowsy and vomiting, with a severe headache. His GCS is 10.

visual.title: Glasgow Coma Scale
visual.label: Now 10
visual.caption: GCS has fallen from normal after the lucid interval.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A blow to the temple, brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval and later deterioration is classic extradural haemorrhage.

steps.x: Loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then deterioration.

elim: Usually follows high-energy injury with no lucid interval, or a slow course in the elderly.
Does not cause progressive deterioration after recovery.
Causes immediate and persistent coma, no lucid interval.
Classically a sudden thunderclap headache, not a lucid interval after a blow to the temple.

steps.x: D: Extradural haemorrhage. LOC, lucid interval, deterioration = extradural haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a left-sided extradural haemorrhage after a fall from a ladder. In the emergency department her GCS falls from 14 to 9 over 40 minutes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination?
o: Bilateral pinpoint pupils with normal limbs
Left fixed dilated pupil with left-sided weakness
Left fixed dilated pupil with right-sided weakness
Right fixed dilated pupil with left-sided weakness
Right ptosis with a small right pupil
questions.e: Extradural haemorrhage classically causes an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil with contralateral weakness.

steps.x: A left-sided bleed with deterioration.

elim: Suggests a pontine lesion or opioids.
Weakness is contralateral to the lesion.
The pupil is ipsilateral to the haematoma.

steps.x: C: Left fixed dilated pupil with right-sided weakness. Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy was hit on the side of the head by a cricket bat 2 hours ago. He was briefly unconscious and then felt fine. He now has a worsening headache and has vomited three times. His GCS is 14 and there is a boggy swelling over the left temple.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his new symptoms?
o: Rising intracranial pressure from an expanding haematoma
questions.e: Headache, vomiting and reduced consciousness after a lucid interval are signs of raised ICP.

clues: briefly unconscious and then felt fine
steps.x: Raised ICP symptoms after a lucid interval.

elim: Causes neck pain and limb signs, not headache and vomiting.
No diarrhoea or contacts; follows head trauma.
Not triggered by head injury with a lucid interval.
Develops over days and does not progress.

steps.x: E: Rising intracranial pressure from an expanding haematoma. Headache, vomiting, reduced GCS = raised ICP from expanding haematoma.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with a known extradural haemorrhage awaiting theatre becomes unresponsive. His BP rises from 128/76 mmHg to 196/102 mmHg, pulse rate falls from 88 bpm to 44 bpm and his breathing becomes irregular with pauses.

visual.title: Observations over 30 minutes
visual.caption: Rising BP with falling pulse: Cushing's response.

questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations form Cushing's triad, signalling brainstem compression and impending herniation.

steps.x: High BP, slow pulse, irregular breathing.

elim: Causes tachycardia, not bradycardia and irregular breathing.

steps.x: C: Impending brain herniation. Cushing's triad = impending herniation, a neurosurgical emergency.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman is hit on the left side of her head by a hockey ball. CT head shows a skull fracture of the left temporal bone with a collection of blood immediately beneath the bone, outside the dura.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of the bleeding?
questions.e: Extradural haemorrhage lies between skull and dura and is most commonly from the middle meningeal artery with a temporal bone fracture.

steps.x: Temporal fracture, blood outside the dura.

elim: Dissection causes stroke, not extradural haematoma.
Intracerebral; not between skull and dura.

steps.x: D: Middle meningeal artery. Temporal bone fracture + extradural blood = middle meningeal artery.

questions.stem: A 23 year old rugby player has an extradural haemorrhage after a kick to the temple. The registrar tells the student most extradural haemorrhages share a pattern of location and vessel type.
questions.q: Which best describes over 95% of extradural haemorrhages?
questions.e: Over 95% of extradural haemorrhages are unilateral supratentorial arterial bleeds.

steps.x: A typical sports injury to the temple.
E: Unilateral, supratentorial and arterial. Over 95%: unilateral, supratentorial, arterial.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with a right temporal extradural haemorrhage has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the emergency department while awaiting transfer to theatre.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the seizure?
questions.e: Seizures are a recognised complication of extradural haemorrhage.

steps.x: Seizure in an acute intracranial bleed.

elim: Occurs 1 to 2 days after stopping drinking.

steps.x: B: Cortical irritation from the haematoma. Complications include seizures, death and permanent deficit.

questions.stem: A 35 year old cyclist fell and hit his left temple. He was fine for 2 hours, then developed headache and drowsiness. His GCS is now 11, his left pupil is larger than the right and sluggish, and his right arm and leg are weaker than the left.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Reduced GCS with a left dilated pupil and right weakness after a left temple blow indicates a left extradural haemorrhage.

clues: right arm and leg are weaker
steps.x: Lateralising signs after a lucid interval.

elim: Not related to trauma with a lucid interval.
The pupil is on the side of the haematoma.
Lacks lateralising signs and lucid interval.

steps.x: A: Left extradural haemorrhage. Pupil side = haematoma side; weakness opposite.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman fell from a horse. She lost consciousness briefly, then talked and walked normally in the ambulance. One hour after arrival her GCS falls to 8.

visual.title: Glasgow Coma Scale
visual.label: Now 8
visual.caption: GCS 8 or below: protect the airway.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Brief LOC, a lucid interval, then rapid deterioration is classic of extradural haemorrhage.

steps.x: The classic three-phase course.

elim: Develops over weeks in the elderly.
Coma from the start, no lucid period.
No history of drinking; follows trauma.
Rapid full recovery without later deterioration.

steps.x: C: Extradural haemorrhage. Lucid interval then deterioration = extradural haemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man was punched on the temple 1 hour ago and was knocked out briefly. He is now alert with GCS 15 but has a headache and has vomited twice.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Urgent non-contrast CT head is the gold standard in suspected extradural haemorrhage.

steps.x: Head injury with LOC and vomiting.

elim: Contrast is not needed and delays diagnosis of acute blood.

steps.x: E: Urgent non-contrast CT head. Urgent non-contrast CT head.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has a CT head after a blow to the right temple. The radiologist reports an extra-axial hyperdense collection.
questions.q: Which CT appearance is most consistent with extradural haemorrhage?
o: Hypodense wedge in the MCA territory
questions.e: Extradural haemorrhage is a lentiform (biconvex) hyperdense collection that does not cross suture lines.

steps.x: An extra-axial bleed after temple trauma.
A: Biconvex collection limited by sutures. Lentiform, biconvex, does not cross sutures.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman on warfarin fell at home and is confused. Her CT head shows a crescent-shaped hyperdense collection over the left hemisphere that crosses the coronal suture but stops at the falx.
questions.q: Which feature most reliably excludes an extradural haemorrhage?
questions.e: Extradural haemorrhage does not cross sutures; subdural crosses sutures but is limited by dural reflections.

steps.x: The collection crosses a suture.

elim: Subdurals are limited by dural reflections; does not exclude.

steps.x: D: Crossing the suture line. Crosses sutures = subdural; stops at sutures = extradural.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man is hit on the temple by a baseball. He has a GCS of 14 and a boggy swelling. A junior doctor suggests a skull X-ray to look for a fracture first.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Non-contrast CT head detects both the temporal fracture and the haematoma; skull X-ray is not used.

steps.x: Suspected temporal fracture and bleed.

elim: Not first-line for suspected extradural haemorrhage.
Shows fracture but misses the haematoma.

steps.x: D: Non-contrast CT head. CT head is the gold standard; skull X-rays are not used.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has an extradural haemorrhage on CT after an assault. His GCS is 14, his airway is patent and his observations are stable.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step in management?
questions.e: The first step is referral to neurosurgery.

steps.x: Confirmed bleed in a stable patient.
D: Refer to neurosurgery. First step: refer to neurosurgery.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with suspected extradural haemorrhage arrives in resus. She has snoring respirations, her GCS is 7 and her oxygen saturation is 91% breathing air.

visual.title: Glasgow Coma Scale
visual.caption: GCS 8 or below: secure the airway.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: Using ABCDE, intubate to protect the airway when consciousness is reduced.

steps.x: A threatened airway with low GCS.
C: Intubation to protect the airway. ABCDE: intubate if GCS low.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with extradural haemorrhage has been intubated and is awaiting theatre. He is lying flat on the trolley.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional measure?
o: Elevate the head and give oxygen
questions.e: Elevate the head, give oxygen and monitor for rising ICP.

steps.x: He is flat while awaiting surgery.

elim: Monitoring for rising ICP is needed.

steps.x: A: Elevate the head and give oxygen. Elevate the head, oxygen, monitor ICP signs.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has a large right temporal lentiform haematoma with midline shift after a fall from a horse. Neurosurgery accepts her.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Definitive management is urgent neurosurgical evacuation by craniotomy or burr hole.

steps.x: A large extradural bleed.

elim: Large haematoma with shift needs surgery.
Steroids are not used in head injury.

steps.x: B: Emergency craniotomy and evacuation. Urgent evacuation via craniotomy or burr hole.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man is undergoing craniotomy for an extradural haemorrhage. After the clot is removed, the surgeon sees a torn vessel actively bleeding in a groove of the inner temporal bone.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional step?
questions.e: Ligating the bleeding artery prevents worsening or recurrence.

clues: groove of the inner temporal bone
steps.x: Middle meningeal artery bleeding.
D: Ligate the middle meningeal artery. Ligate the bleeding artery.

questions.stem: A 20 year old man with an extradural haemorrhage is deteriorating rapidly in a hospital without neurosurgery. Transfer will take 2 hours and his left pupil is now fixed and dilated. Neurosurgery advises immediate local decompression.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate procedure?
questions.e: Burr hole decompression is an option when craniotomy is not immediately available.

clues: left pupil is now fixed and dilated
steps.x: Rapid deterioration far from neurosurgery.

elim: Pupil change means herniation is imminent.

steps.x: B: Burr hole decompression. Craniotomy or burr hole decompression.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boxer has an extradural haemorrhage after a punch to the side of his head. A student asks why a blow to this particular area causes this bleed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Bridging veins tear with shearing forces
The dura is loose at the pterion
The middle meningeal artery runs near the pterion in a groove of thin bone
The sigmoid sinus lies under the temple
questions.e: The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove of the inner temporal bone near the pterion, so a fracture lacerates it.

steps.x: A temple blow.
D: The middle meningeal artery runs near the pterion in a groove of thin bone. Pterion: thin bone over the middle meningeal artery.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman's CT after a temple injury shows a biconvex hyperdense collection. A student asks why it has this shape.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Brain tissue compressing the clot into a crescent
High-pressure arterial blood confined by dura adherent at sutures
questions.e: Arterial blood strips the dura but is confined by suture attachments, producing a lentiform shape.

steps.x: Lentiform shape on CT.

elim: Not the reason for the shape.

steps.x: C: High-pressure arterial blood confined by dura adherent at sutures. Arterial pressure + adherent dura at sutures = lentiform.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man had a brief loss of consciousness after a blow to the head and then seemed completely well for 3 hours before collapsing. His father asks how he could seem fine.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: He had a second head injury
The haematoma took time to reach a critical volume
questions.e: The lucid interval reflects time for the expanding haematoma to reach a critical volume before ICP rises.

steps.x: A lucid interval.
E: The haematoma took time to reach a critical volume. Lucid interval = time to critical volume before ICP rises.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a left extradural haemorrhage. His left pupil becomes fixed and dilated. A student asks about the cause.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Direct trauma to the optic nerve
Uncal herniation compressing the oculomotor nerve
questions.e: The uncus herniates through the tentorial notch, compressing CN III and its parasympathetic fibres, causing an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil.

clues: left pupil becomes fixed and dilated
steps.x: Ipsilateral pupil dilation.

elim: Causes visual loss and RAPD, not a fixed dilated pupil from herniation.

steps.x: E: Uncal herniation compressing the oculomotor nerve. Uncal herniation compresses CN III parasympathetic fibres.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man with an extradural haemorrhage develops a BP of 200/110 mmHg, a pulse rate of 40 bpm and irregular breathing. A student asks why this matters.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Brainstem compression from raised intracranial pressure
questions.e: Cushing's triad is a late sign of brainstem compression and impending herniation.

steps.x: Cushing's triad.

elim: Not related to the head injury.

steps.x: A: Brainstem compression from raised intracranial pressure. Cushing's triad = brainstem compression, impending herniation.
